claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles can possess high configurational entropy and a random solid-solution structure.
High configurational entropy stabilizes a random solid-solution phase at operating temperatures.
High surface-to-volume ratio enhances surface diffusion in near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
Enhanced surface diffusion promotes atomic reordering and elemental segregation.
The balance between configurational-entropy stabilization and surface-diffusion-driven segregation governs nanoparticle structural and chemical stability.
A thin inert passivation layer reduces surface atomic mobility and effective surface diffusion.
Increasing particle size reduces the effective surface-area contribution to segregation.
Reducing surface mobility sustains a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Reducing surface mobility mitigates phase separation and the formation of segregated chemical domains.
Passivated nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation than composition- and size-matched uncoated nanoparticles after identical heat treatment.
Passivated nanoparticles will preserve phase integrity better than uncoated nanoparticles after identical heat treatment.
Better preservation of composition and phase integrity will produce more stable catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Uncoated nanoparticles will undergo more pronounced segregation or structural degradation under the same thermal conditions.
The proposed stability mechanism applies over 773–1173 K for catalytic service and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric service.
Using an inert or controlled atmosphere reduces extraneous chemical effects during thermal testing.
The hypothesis may not apply to systems with substantially different surface chemistry, particle size, or additional thermochemical effects.
The magnitude of the passivation effect depends on the passivating layer and detailed interatomic interactions.
